searchText: Hi <@552133098075193354>! 🙂 Wanted to check on the usage of eth_getBlockByNumber + finalized and latest flags.............. - The two flags which are available are the finalized (not reorg-able) and latest (reorg-able) yeap? - Did the "safe/unsafe" flags got dropped off along the way? Cheers! Safe will be available on geth soon, pr is already there. Unsafe was dropped afaik `safe` will be set to the most recent *justified* block right after the merge which is pretty safe, and then there is a plan to improve on this value in a way which would make it pretty close to the head. `unsafe` tag has gone, and `latest` remains returning the head of the chain which should be used with care as it's unsafe reorg-wise I find it very weird so much engineering effort is being put into the to idea someone can suddenly double the hashrate and hit TTD too quickly. If someone had that capability, Ethereum would already be unsecured. Seems like a no brainer the easier solution is the one where the correct TTD is baked into the release to reduce human error and ensure a much smoother merge. And in the event this magical entity can double the hashrate, you can see it coming and coordinate to push the TTD out with an override as an emergency move Are there any reliable charts on total ETH hash rate over time? If we were down more than 50% off the peak, then I could see a stronger argument that there exists out in the ether enough machines to suddenly double the hashrate https://www.coinwarz.com/mining/ethereum/hashrate-chart maybe? So there's 0.3 PH that "went missing". We've seen ASICS and GPUs dumped on the street and on the market. How much of this hashrate is now actually trashed and how much is waiting "in the wings" is unknowable. And in a month some more hashrate, some 10%?, will fall off, because DAG increase ^ that 0.3PH drop looks _very_ close to the grey glacier fork date, enough to suspect its not a coincidence Systematically, IMO, all attack vectors should be scored via a risk assessment method to determine the best course of action. We should be in a situation whereby the weighted overall risk of an attack is met with an appropriate level of response. Of course, quantifying these will be notoriously difficult for some attack vectors, but it can be done. Someone doubling hashrate on one of the biggest and most decentralized crypto seems to score quite low in the feasibility of attack, but it is quite criticalif it were to happen. There is essentially no engineering effort being put into this. It is entirely a discussion. All paths are approximately equal in terms of engineering, and allare incredibly similar to each other. I agree that while there is no engineering effort being put into it, I do I think we are getting bogged down (a distraction) on testnet hashrate manipulation that is not possible on mainnet. I would expect the tom foolery to only increase from miners as we get closer to the merge where profitability is so low that moving to a testnet for a few days does not matter. The solution is quite simple, if possible; change the testnet client TTD to a more smoothing calculation so it is relatively unaffected by large changes in hashrate. While this might be cheating, we know this part of the current TTD is solid and can be shipped with the mainnet release. This way we can move forward instead of spending too much time trying to figure out how to stop miners from slowing down the merge rollout until they figure out another way. That is significantly more engineering effort than any of the options on the table right now, and I think everyone is against having the goerli code change at all at this point. At least there's strong opinions! I hope everyone brings their A-game to the consensus call 😅 Gray Glacier affected difficulty, but not network hashrate At the end it is the difficulty bomb, not hashrate bomb And that hashrate was vanished with the ETH price drop Mining is not really profitable right now unless you have very cheap electricity We're hosting some panels and round-table discussions on post-merge MEV in Paris Since many of the client teams are testing mev-boost, I thought you might be interested feel free to DM for details - short writeup here https://medium.com/p/dc31df8baaf7 Right but my assumption is that some large cohort of miners opted not to update for GG and instead chose the fork as a time to exit (or worse forgot about or otherwise didn't prepare for the fork). 300 TH/s is a lot of hashpower. No way they mined for that long without upgrading. it just feels very coincidental that the drop happened within a couple hours of the fork. if the timestamps are correct the drop was ~2-3h _after_ the fork though which would imply that they upgraded. Which is equally weird, if you were planning on dropping 300TH why wait for the fork? Look at the ETH price chart It just coincided with Gray Glacier and we're trusting that we won't need a TTD adjustment last minute....

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: `safe` will be set to the most recent *justified* block right after the merge which is pretty safe, and then there is a plan to improve on this value in a way which would make it pretty close to the head. `unsafe` tag has gone, and `latest` remains returning the head of the chain which should be used with care as it's unsafe reorg-wise

excerpts.author: sharkhuh
excerpts.content:
I find it very weird so much engineering effort is being put into the to idea someone can suddenly double the hashrate and hit TTD too quickly. If someone had that capability, Ethereum would already be unsecured.

Seems like a no brainer the easier solution is the one where the correct TTD is baked into the release to reduce human error and ensure a much smoother merge.

And in the event this magical entity can double the hashrate, you can see it coming and coordinate to push the TTD out with an override as an emergency move
